analysis.one_liner: Gives managed-care patients guaranteed appeals, direct access to specialists and emergency care, and the right to sue their plan.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on May 14, 2001 and placed on the Senate calendar the next day, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was one of the 'patients' bill of rights' bills of 2001. It would have required health plans to run utilization review under strict rules, decide claims on set deadlines, and give patients internal appeals plus a binding review by an independent outside medical reviewer. It would also have guaranteed direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, emergency care without prior approval, coverage for clinical trials, and new rights to sue health plans. The Senate read it twice, put it on the calendar, and never brought it to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People covered by HMOs and other managed-care plans. The bill would have guaranteed a decision on prior authorization within 14 days (72 hours when a doctor certifies urgency), an internal appeal, and a binding independent external review; plans that ignored an external reviewer's ruling could owe up to $1,000 a day in penalties. It would have let patients see an OB-GYN or pediatrician without a gatekeeper referral, get emergency care at in-network cost-sharing without prior authorization, reach a specialist outside the network at no extra cost when no in-network specialist is qualified, and get covered care in approved clinical trials. It also barred plans from paying reviewers in ways that encourage claim denials, and created federal lawsuit rights against plans that wrongly deny or delay care.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must decide prior-authorization requests within 14 days (28 days from the claim), expedite decisions within 72 hours when a doctor certifies urgency, and treat a missed deadline as a denial that can be appealed. [S3]

Every denial comes with an internal appeal reviewed by someone not involved in the first decision, and then a right to an independent external review by a certified entity with no ties to the plan; the external reviewer's decision is binding on the plan, which must authorize coverage within the reviewer's stated timeframe. [S3]

Plans that refuse to follow an external review determination can face up to $1,000 per day in civil penalties against the person refusing the benefit, a $10,000 penalty paid to the patient, attorney's fees, and additional penalties up to $500,000 for repeated patterns of refusal. [S3]

Patients may designate any available participating primary care provider, see an OB-GYN or pediatrician directly, get emergency services without prior authorization under a 'prudent layperson' standard with no more cost-sharing than in-network care, and obtain out-of-network specialty care at no extra cost when no qualified in-network specialist is available. [S3]

Plans must cover routine costs for patients in approved clinical trials, a minimum hospital stay after a mastectomy, and cannot compensate employees or contractors in ways that encourage denial of claims, interfere with doctor-patient communications, or discourage patient advocacy. [S3]
The bill adds civil remedies (Sec. 302) against plans under the federal benefits law ERISA, creating a route to court for patients whose claims are wrongly denied or delayed. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed-care plans would bear the compliance costs, the cost of external reviews, and new lawsuit exposure; employers that fund their own plans could also be sued. Plans could pass some of this to premiums, and patients choosing a point-of-service option outside the plan's network would bear any added premium or cost-sharing themselves.

drawbacks.text: The new lawsuit rights under ERISA would expose insurers and self-insured employers to litigation; the industry and many employers argued this would raise premiums and could lead some employers to drop coverage — the central fight that sank the 2001 patients' rights effort. [S3]
Under the consumer choice option, any added premium and cost-sharing for coverage outside the plan's network is borne by the enrollee, not the plan. [S3]
Patients must pay up to a $25 filing fee to start an external review, waived only for indigent patients or when the plan waives internal review. [S3]

The bill bundles unrelated provisions, including extension of customs user fees through 2011 and a one-day shift in the timing of Medicare payments, which are revenue offsets rather than patient protections. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For someone whose HMO denies or stalls needed care, the guaranteed deadlines, binding outside review, and penalties for ignoring it address a real and common problem, and the access rules end some of the most resented managed-care practices. The honest cost is the right to sue: it is what gives the appeal system teeth, but it is also the provision insurers and employers most opposed on the grounds that litigation costs reach premiums, and it is the reason parallel bills stalled in conference. The bundling of customs-fee revenue into a health bill is unrelated filler.

outcome.mechanism: McCain introduced the bill, the Senate read it twice and put it on the calendar the next day, and the chamber never called it up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 14, 2001 by Senator McCain for himself, Senators Edwards and Kennedy. [S3]
On May 15, 2001 it was read a second time and placed on the Senate legislative calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 42. [S5]
No further action appears in the bill's record after May 15, 2001; it sat on the calendar and never received a Senate vote. [S5]
The bill's latest available text is the version placed on the calendar, and no committee history is listed for it. [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed-care insurers and the employers who sponsor health plans are better off because the bill died: they avoided the binding external-review mandates, the daily penalties for ignoring review decisions, and the new federal right to sue. Patients in HMOs gained nothing from the outcome; the appeal protections and access guarantees never took effect.

against.name: Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Never brought S. 872 to the floor; the Senate's patients'-rights effort moved instead through a competing bipartisan bill, leaving this one on the calendar.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Threatened to veto patients'-rights legislation containing a broad right to sue health plans, pressing Congress toward a narrower version and against the bill's central enforcement provision.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and managed-care plans and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the patients'-rights bills' new lawsuit rights and appeal mandates, which would have exposed plans to binding external review and litigation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Senate Republican with two Senate Democrats, and the patients'-rights fight cut across party lines — the divide was over how far the right to sue should go, not over party sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped plans of discretion over denied claims through binding external review, imposed daily penalties for refusing reviewer-ordered care, and let patients sue in federal court. Insurers opposed these provisions because litigation and compliance costs reach premiums and profits.
The ERISA civil remedies would have made self-insured employers the target of the same lawsuits, a cost employers warned would push them to drop or trim coverage.

The bill would have created a federally certified industry of external review entities, paid by plans, to re-decide denied claims. Its interests run with patients' access to appeal, though it profits from the process itself.
Emergency care without prior authorization, at in-network cost-sharing, plus required post-stabilization reimbursement, would have reduced unpaid emergency bills and disputes over coverage.
New federal causes of action against health plans would have generated litigation work, with attorney's fees available to prevailing patients.
